Before you start

Students learn how a feed drifts toward "alpha" content, test three of its claims against research, and name one low-key move for when a joke goes too far. Describe the content without playing clips, respect the want for confidence and respect, and keep any student who seems angry and alone for a quiet check-in after.

Every student in the room

Don't make the boys the problem and the girls the audience, and remember that family and faith shape what "being a man" means without that being contempt for women.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Open with a few “sound familiar” moments: you watched a few videos about lifting or making money, and now your feed explains what women “really” want. Someone gets called “soft” or a “simp” for texting a girl back like a normal person. Then: “Today is about how this content reaches you, why it works, and what the research says about its claims. Nobody’s in trouble for what’s in their feed, and we’re not naming anyone.” Everyone in the room is part of this, whatever their gender.

Slide 2 · Notes

Take a few guesses out loud, or collect them and read the range. The next slide shows the number.

Slide 3 · Notes

Toxic content in this study meant alpha-male, anti-women, reactionary or conspiracy videos. The point: it feels like you found it yourself. It was delivered.

Slide 4 · Notes

Walk the steps quickly. Confidence and respect are good things to want. The package and the monthly fee are the catch. “Beta” and “brainwashed” are built to stop you thinking for yourself. Ask students to keep one question in their pocket: what does this person want me to feel, and what do they want me to buy?

Slide 5 · Notes

Students stand if they think it’s true, or raise a hand from their seat if they’d rather. Ask one person standing and one sitting why. The next slide shows the research.

Slide 6 · Notes

The biologist who made “alpha wolf” famous has spent years saying the term is misleading.

Slide 7 · Notes

Students stand if they think it’s true, or raise a hand from their seat if they’d rather. Ask one person standing and one sitting why. The next slide shows the research.

Slide 8 · Notes

Looks and money mattered; they just weren’t on top, for men or women.

Slide 9 · Notes

Students stand if they think it’s true, or raise a hand from their seat if they’d rather. Ask one person standing and one sitting why. The next slide shows the research.

Slide 10 · Notes

This content lands partly because it offers a team and someone to blame. Reaching out first and making plans are skills guys build now.

Slide 11 · Notes

Everyone writes two things. Collect, shuffle, tally both out loud. The next slide shows what usually happens.

Slide 12 · Notes

If your tally doesn’t show the gap, say so honestly and ask why someone might go along with a joke they don’t like.

Slide 13 · Notes

Lead with what students bring: family, faith and culture shape what being a man means, and traditional roles are not the same thing as contempt for women. Not everyone has a man at home, so say “from anyone in your life.” This works whatever your gender. Avoid “In X families” generalizations.

Slide 14 · Notes

Jokes are how a group tests what’s okay. If everyone laughs or nobody says anything, the line moves further next time. No speech needed, and these work for anyone in the group, whatever their gender. Two to skip: laughing along to keep the peace, and roasting the guy in the group chat. He needs a friend, not an audience.

Slide 15 · Notes

Pairs talk it through, then a few share. Earbuds in feels easier, but it reads as agreement. The next slide shows one good move.

Slide 16 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 17 · Notes

Pairs decide. Sending more clips or roasting him both keep him there. The next slide shows one good move.

Slide 18 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 19 · Notes

Pairs decide. Close with: “You won’t always get it right. One honest ‘nah’ is more than most people say.” The next slide shows one good move.

Slide 20 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 21 · Notes

Turn and talk, partners by seat. The money pitch lands harder when money is tight; rules can feel like relief to someone who finds social rules hard to read; a breakup or loneliness opens the door. And people draw on family, faith, friends, a coach. Nobody speaks for a group.

Slide 22 · Notes

Students write for themselves; nobody shares. Share the student page link. It has the claims, the moves, and when to get an adult involved.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain how a feed drifts toward "alpha" and anti-women content, test three of its claims against the research, and name one low-key move for when a joke in the group goes too far. Wanting confidence and respect is treated as fair; nobody is shamed for what their feed shows them.

Materials

  • Scraps of paper for the opening guess and the anonymous agree/disagree cards
  • Index cards or notebooks for the private exit question
  • The student page link (last slide) to share after advisory

Flow

  1. 2 minOpen: you didn't search for it
  2. 3 minHow fast does a feed drift? (written guess)
  3. 4 minClaims vs. the research (stand up, sit down)
  4. 3 minWhat most guys think (anonymous cards)
  5. 2 minSilence sounds like agreement
  6. 4 minThree moments (pairs)
  7. 2 minWhat you want to keep (private) and the student page

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

The feed guess (3), anonymous agree/disagree cards (3), the low-key moves and one moment in pairs (3), the student page link (1). The student page has the claims, the feed settings and when to get an adult.

Before you teach
Respect the want.

Confidence, strength, money, respect and not being lonely are good things to want, and that's how this content gets in. If a student gets defensive or quotes a creator, stay steady: "Wanting confidence and respect makes total sense. The question is what gets you there." Students who feel lectured stop listening.

Don't play clips in class.

Describe the content; don't show it. Keep the talk about content and situations, never named students. Some students in the circle follow these creators, and some have friends who do.

Girls and students of every gender are in the room.

This content is about many of them. Don't ask girls to explain how it feels or to debate a guy who repeats it. Say plainly that muting and blocking are always okay, and that nobody owes anyone a debate.

Know what goes to an adult the same day.

Someone sharing photos of a real person, real or AI-made. Threats. Talk about a girl that turns into a plan to hurt, follow or embarrass her. Don't ask about these in the circle. Follow up with a counselor or dean that day.

Watch for the student who seems alone.

A student who seems much angrier lately, or who says these videos are the only place that gets him, may need a counselor more than a debate. Check in privately afterward. Don't ask self-harm questions in the circle; any disclosure goes to a counselor, and 988 (call or text) is open any time.

Stay out of party politics.

Families hold a wide range of views about men's and women's roles, often rooted in faith or culture. Keep the conversation on how feeds work and what the research says about specific claims, and leave room for students to respect the adults who raised them.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Don't make the boys the problem and the girls the audience.

Most guys are less into this than they seem, and that's the core of the lesson. Girls, nonbinary students and boys all get pulled by feeds, and anyone can be the one who says "nah." Boys can be scared, lonely and tender; girls can be ambitious and loud. Keep examples off stereotypes in both directions.

"Soft," "simp" and anti-gay jokes police every guy.

Gay, bi, trans and questioning students hear these words as being about them, and straight guys get boxed in by them too. Name them as pressure. Partners in examples can be anyone; the Jade card is one example, not the only kind of relationship. Know where to point students: a counselor and The Trevor Project (call 1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678).

Family, culture and faith shape what "being a man" means.

People students respect may define it differently, and traditional roles are not the same thing as contempt for women. Avoid "In X families" generalizations. The closing question is private: which parts of what you were taught do you want to keep?

Not every student has a man at home.

Some are raised by a single mom, grandparents, two moms, or in foster or kinship care. When you ask what they were taught about being a man, say "from anyone in your life": a coach, an uncle, an older cousin, a friend's dad, or nobody in particular.

The money pitch lands harder when money is tight.

Get-rich and "high-value" content can feel like a way out for students whose families are struggling, and the courses cost real money every month. Keep the good part: lift, study, save, build discipline. None of that costs anything or requires the package.

Rules can feel like relief.

Some students, including some autistic students, find unwritten social rules hard to read, and content that promises clear rules about dating and status can feel like help. Treat that want as fair and point to real support. For stand up, sit down, let students vote with a hand or thumb from their seat.

What the research says

Researchers set up ten fresh phones with accounts posing as 16- and 18-year-old boys. Some searched only for gym, sports and gaming. Every account was shown misogynistic or "alpha" content within 23 minutes.

Baker, Ging and Andreasen, Dublin City University, 2024

In that study, toxic content meant alpha-male, anti-women, reactionary or conspiracy videos. It was a small study, but it matches what other researchers have found.

Baker, Ging and Andreasen, 2024

The biologist who helped make "alpha wolf" famous studied wild wolves for 13 summers and concluded a typical pack is a family: two parents and their young. The ranking picture came mostly from unrelated wolves in captivity, and he has since called the term misleading.

Mech, Canadian Journal of Zoology, 1999

Across 10,047 people in 37 cultures, both men and women ranked "kind and understanding" and "intelligent" above earning power and good looks, in every sample.

Buss, Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 1989

College men overestimated how sexist the other men in the room were. After seeing the real numbers, their estimates of other men's sexism were lower three weeks later.

Kilmartin et al., Sex Roles, 2008

In a 2021 national survey, 15% of American men said they had no close friends, up from 3% in 1990.

Cox, Survey Center on American Life, 2021
